title: Vivek Wadhwa Urges U.S. to Scrap H-1B and Replace It With a Startup Visa
excerpt: The Indian-American tech investor argues Americans have legitimate grievances about H-1B abuse and proposes a startup visa as an alternative that rewards job creators.
body:
• Indian-American investor Vivek Wadhwa calls for scrapping the H-1B visa and replacing it with a dedicated startup visa for entrepreneurs who create American jobs
  • Wadhwa says Americans are justified in their frustration with what he describes as unethical exploitation of the visa system by some Indian IT firms
  • He notes that obtaining a green card, which took him 18 months in the 1980s, would now take an Indian applicant approximately 70 years
  • The comments come as the Trump administration proposes new restrictions including eliminating the 60-day grace period for laid-off H-1B workers

Indian-American tech investor and academic Vivek Wadhwa has called on the United States to abandon the H-1B visa program and replace it with a startup visa, arguing that Americans have legitimate reasons to resent how the system has been exploited, according to The Times of India.

Wadhwa, a distinguished fellow at Harvard Law School and adjunct professor at Carnegie Mellon University's School of Engineering in Silicon Valley, said the U.S. should redirect its immigration framework toward attracting entrepreneurs who build companies and create jobs rather than maintaining a system he believes enables wage suppression and outsourcing abuse.

A Longtime Advocate Turns Blunt

Wadhwa has spent decades studying the contributions of immigrants to the American economy, but his latest remarks mark a sharper acknowledgment of public frustration. He said Americans "rightfully hate" what he described as unethical practices by some Indian nationals and firms that exploit the H-1B system, according to the report.

https://x.com/SanDiegoKnight/status/2091190937687105783

The H-1B visa, designed to help U.S. companies fill specialized roles they cannot staff domestically, has long drawn criticism. Detractors argue that Indian IT outsourcing firms use the program to import cheaper labor rather than genuinely scarce talent. Wadhwa's proposed startup visa would shift the focus from employer-sponsored temporary workers to founders building companies on American soil.

"Innovation is globalised and stupid policies trying to keep people out will only keep innovation out."

— Vivek Wadhwa, Indian-American Investor and Academic

The Green Card Bottleneck

Central to Wadhwa's argument is the broken path from temporary visa to permanent residency. He has said that when he arrived in the United States in the 1980s, obtaining a green card took roughly 18 months. For an Indian applicant today, the backlog stretches to an estimated 70 years due to per-country caps that disproportionately affect nationals from high-demand countries.

"They can't get green cards... they're worried about getting kicked out any day... who wants to come here like this?" Wadhwa said in an earlier interview, describing how uncertainty discourages skilled immigrants from committing to the United States long-term.

The backlog currently exceeds one million Indian applicants, creating what immigration advocates have termed a system of "indentured servitude" where workers remain tethered to sponsoring employers for decades, unable to change jobs or negotiate higher wages without losing their place in the queue.

Policy Shifts Add Pressure

Wadhwa's comments arrive amid an escalating series of immigration restrictions from the Trump administration. The Department of Homeland Security recently proposed eliminating the 60-day grace period that allows H-1B workers to find new employment after a job loss. Separately, officials are weighing a $100,000 fee on foreign student work programs, and DHS has expanded H-1B fees to include extension petitions, adding thousands of dollars in costs for employers.

Wadhwa has argued that India still produces engineers and scientists with deep expertise in fields like plasma physics, thermodynamics, and electrical engineering that the U.S. startup ecosystem increasingly lacks. But visa hurdles block the talent pipeline. His own company now plans to pilot technology in India first before bringing it to the United States — a reversal he has described as emblematic of a broader shift in where innovation happens.

What a Startup Visa Could Look Like

Wadhwa has long advocated giving H-1B preference to direct employees of technology companies rather than third-party staffing agencies. A startup visa would go further by creating a pathway specifically for founders who raise capital, create jobs, and build businesses in the United States.

Several immigration reform proposals have included startup visa provisions over the years, but none has passed Congress. The concept has bipartisan appeal in principle — it targets job creators rather than job seekers — but has consistently stalled amid broader partisan gridlock on immigration.

For the Indian diaspora, Wadhwa's argument presents an uncomfortable duality: acknowledging real abuses within a system that has also been the primary gateway for hundreds of thousands of skilled Indian professionals to build careers and lives in the United States. Whether his call for a wholesale replacement gains traction will depend on whether policymakers can separate reform from restriction in an increasingly polarized environment.
